opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things going on at once. The first is a selection effect in how benchmarks get built. When people design a benchmark, they usually want it to be hard enough that current models score poorly, but not so hard that scores sit at zero, because a benchmark where everything gets zero doesn't tell you anything and nobody will adopt it. So benchmarks tend to be pitched just beyond the current frontier. If capabilities improve at all quickly, you'd naturally expect them to cross that gap within a year or two.

The second is that benchmarks tend to measure fairly narrow, well-specified tasks: things with clear right answers that you can grade automatically, like multiple-choice questions, math problems with numerical answers, or coding problems with unit tests. Those are exactly the kinds of tasks current training methods are best at. You can do reinforcement learning against them, you can generate lots of similar data, and labs have a strong incentive to optimize for whatever benchmarks get reported. So there's a sort of Goodhart dynamic where the benchmark gets saturated faster than the underlying capability it was meant to proxy actually improves.

And I think that's the more important point. Benchmark saturation can give a somewhat misleading impression of how close we are to systems that can do most economically valuable work. The things that are hard to put in a benchmark, like long-horizon agency, operating in messy real-world environments with unclear objectives, coordinating with other people over weeks or months, and knowing what to do when nobody has told you what the task is, are also the things models are still relatively weak at. If you look at the actual economic impact of AI so far, it's much smaller than you'd guess from looking at benchmark scores alone.

So my view is that fast saturation partly reflects real progress, but it also reflects that we keep building benchmarks in the region of task-space where models are strongest. That's why I'm somewhat skeptical of arguments that go from "models now beat experts on this hard exam" to "we're a couple of years from full automation of remote work." There's a big gap between those two things, and benchmarks systematically underweight it.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks are designed just beyond the current frontier and that improving models would likely cross that gap within a year or two, attributing rapid saturation partly to benchmarks being within reach.

r002.rationale: It mentions labs’ incentive to optimize for reported benchmarks, but does not identify lab funding as selecting for benchmarks expected to be useful soon.

r003.rationale: It says a benchmark where every model scores zero “doesn't tell you anything,” conveying that it offers no useful signal.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are a few things going on, and they're kind of layered on top of each other.

The first one is just selection. When people build a benchmark, they're trying to capture something that models can't do yet, but they also need the benchmark to be useful, which means it has to be in a regime where you can actually measure progress. So you end up targeting tasks that are just beyond the frontier, not tasks that are ten years beyond the frontier. If you made a benchmark that was really far out, nobody would score above zero on it and it would be useless for a long time. So there's a natural pressure toward building benchmarks that are close to being solved, and then, unsurprisingly, they get solved.

The second thing is that benchmarks are usually much narrower than the capability they're supposed to be a proxy for. You want to measure something like "can the model do math," but what you actually have is a few thousand problems with a particular distribution, a particular format, a particular style of answer. And once a benchmark becomes prominent, labs optimize for it, sometimes deliberately and sometimes just because the data that resembles it ends up in training sets. So the gap between "does well on the benchmark" and "has the underlying capability" can open up, and the benchmark saturates faster than the capability actually improves. That's part of why I think it's always worth being a little suspicious when a benchmark goes from, say, twenty percent to ninety percent in a year. Some of that is real, but some of it is just that the benchmark stopped being a good measurement instrument.

And then the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that the rate of progress genuinely has been fast. If you're spending compute at the scale labs have been spending it, and the scaling trends hold up at all, then you should expect capabilities to move a lot in a year or two. So even a well-constructed benchmark that isn't being gamed will saturate on a timescale of a couple of years, because that's just how fast things are moving. It's not only an artifact of bad benchmark design.

The thing I'd add is that saturation doesn't mean the models are now good at everything in that domain. A lot of the benchmarks are short, self-contained problems, and the models get very good at those while still struggling with longer, messier tasks that require keeping track of a lot of context or working for hours without making a mistake. So I'd read fast saturation partly as a sign that we've been measuring the wrong thing, and we should be moving toward evaluations that look more like actual work, where the task takes a long time and there's no clean answer key.

r001.rationale: It says benchmark builders target tasks just beyond the current frontier because tasks far beyond it would remain unsolved, making the benchmark useless for a long time.

r002.rationale: The response discusses choosing benchmarks that can measure progress soon, but does not attribute that choice to lab funding.

r003.rationale: It explains that if nobody scores above zero, the benchmark would be useless for a long time, conveying that it cannot serve as a useful measure of progress.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of reasons. One is that a benchmark is a fixed target. Once it becomes popular, people spend a lot of effort improving performance on it, both explicitly and through the kinds of data and training methods they use. So progress on that benchmark can be much faster than progress on the broader capability it was intended to measure. That doesn't necessarily mean anyone is cheating; it's just that a measurable target attracts optimization.

The other reason is that benchmarks often don't have much headroom. You design a set of questions that current models find difficult, but if capabilities are improving quickly, those questions might stop being difficult in a year or two. Once models are getting nearly everything right, the benchmark can't distinguish a somewhat better model from a dramatically better one.

And there's a selection effect: we're especially interested in benchmarks where models are starting to make progress. A benchmark where every model gets zero isn't very useful for comparing them, so it tends to get less attention. That means the benchmarks we're watching are often already in the part of the improvement curve where saturation is approaching.

So I wouldn't interpret saturation as meaning that AI has solved the whole underlying domain. It often means we've exhausted the measuring instrument.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks attract attention when models are already making progress, but does not say benchmarks are created when solving them appears within reach.

r002.rationale: It does not mention lab funding or funding favoring benchmarks expected to be useful soon.

r003.rationale: It says all-zero benchmarks are not useful for comparing models, but does not identify their lack of internal signal for development decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a couple of things going on. One is that a benchmark is usually designed around what’s challenging for models at the time it’s created. But if capabilities are improving rapidly, something that looks very difficult today can become quite easy in a couple of years. And creating a good benchmark takes time, so you’re always somewhat behind the frontier.

The other thing is that benchmarks become targets. People use them to guide model development, so progress on those particular tasks can be faster than progress on the broader capability you were trying to measure. That doesn’t necessarily mean anyone is cheating. You can just make lots of reasonable development decisions based on benchmark performance, and eventually the benchmark becomes less informative.

And saturation doesn’t mean the underlying problem is solved. A model might get almost every question right on a fixed test but still be unreliable when you change the setting or ask it to carry out a much longer task. So I’d distinguish between exhausting a particular measurement and exhausting the room for improvement in the capability itself.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks target what is challenging when created and can become easy as capabilities improve, but does not say creators choose benchmarks because solving them already appears within reach.

r002.rationale: It discusses development decisions guided by benchmark results, but does not identify lab funding or near-term usefulness as a selection pressure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss benchmarks where all models score zero or explain their lack of value as an internal development signal.
